lawyer:
Kazi Md Shafiqul Hasan Advocate-For the Petitioner 
Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan, Advocate-For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Amal Krishna Biswas ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Pulin Kamar Das ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued at the instance of the pre-emptee petitioner calling upon the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 15-3-2009 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Jessore in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 81 of 2007 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 8-11-2007 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Bagharpara, Jessore in Miscellaneous Case No. 23 of 2005 should not be set aside.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the instant Rule are that on 19-6-2005 the predecessor of the opposite-party No. 1 as pre-emptor filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 being Miscellaneous Case No. 23 of 2005 before the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Bagharpara, Jessore for pre-empting the case land measuring 5 decimals appertaining to SA Khatian No. 39, Plot No. 626 (old), and No. 951 (present) of Mouza Dogachhia under Police Station Bagharpara, District Jessore.

3. The case of the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1, in brief, is that the lands of case jote originally belonged to SA recorded tenants Paresh Chandra Das and Bhupendra Nath Das; that Paresh Chandra died leaving behind Dhiren, Niren, the original pre-emptor Pulin Kumar Das and the vendor Ananta Kumar Das as his legal heirs; that Niren transferred his share to his brother Pulin Kumar Das, the original pre-emptor by a registered sale deed dated 22-1-1995. Bhupendra Nath died leaving behind the proforma opposite parties as his heirs. The pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance as well as by purchase in the case jote and he came to learn about the impugned sale on 2-6-2005 when the preemptee came to the case land to take possession thereof. Thereafter, on 15-6-2005 the pre-emptor became sanguine about the transfer of the case land after obtaining the certified copy of the impugned sale deed. The preemptee is completely a stranger to the case land and the pre-emptor had no knowledge about the impugned sale and the case and is extremely necessary for the proper and better enjoyment and possession of his other adjacent land and hence, the pre-emption case.

4. The case of the pre-emptee-petitioner is that without cause of action the case is bad for defect of parties, barred by limitation and the case land along with other lands originally belonged to three brothers, namely Bhejal Mondal, Sharat Mondal and Bharat Mondal in equal shares and SA Khatian No. 34 was correctly prepared and finally published in their names. Bhejal Mondal died leaving behind one daughter named Laxibala Bhoumik as his sole heir. Thereafter Bharat Mondal died behind his brother Sharat Mondal to succeed his estate and then Sharat Mondal died leaving behind his widow and the preemptee as his heirs. Out of necessity for money, the mother of the pre-emptee mortgaged 37 decimals of land from the case jote to Amullya Sarker and Bijoy Krishna Sarker by a registered deed of patta and subsequently, SA record was prepared in the name of the said Amullya Sarker and Bijoy Krishna Sarker. Although the mortgage money was repaid, a redemption deed could not be executed due to financial crisis of the pre-emptee and his mother. The SA Khatian prepared and published in the name of Amullya Sarker and Bijoy Krishna Sarker is erroneous and the pre-emptee had no knowledge about the said khatian. The pre-emptee is in possession of 49 decimals of land in the case jote by inheritance and as such he is a co-sharer in the same. The pre-emptor had full knowledge about the impugned sale and that he has no necessity to pre-empt the case land and thereof, the application for pre-emption is liable to be dismissed.

5. The pre-emptor examined 2 P.W.s including himself as PW 1 and the pre-emptee cross-examined them in detail. The pre-emptor exhibited the impugned sale deed dated 2-6-2005, SA Khatian No. 39 and the sale deed dated 22-1-1995 as Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Although the examination-in-chief of the pre-emptee as OPW 1 was recorded in part, he did not turn up before the trial Court to complete his remaining examination-in-chief, the cross-examination and accordingly, no other documentary evidence was produced by him to substantiate his defence case as contended in his written objection.

6. Upon assessment of the application for pre-emption, written objection, evidence and other materials on record, the trial Court allowed pre-emption holding, inter alia, that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance and by purchase in the case holding and the case is not barred by limitation and not bad for defect of parties. The lower appellate Court also concurred with the findings and decision of the trial Court in all material points reiterating that the pre-emptor-petitioner is a co-sharer in the case jote whereas the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1 is a complete stranger to the same and that the pre-emptee had no valid reasons to oppose the pre-emption sought and his defence case being unreasonable, unmeritcious and vexatious, the Court of appeal below dismissed the appeal with a cost of Taka 2,000.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with impugned judgment and order passed by the appellate Court with the above concurrent judgments, the pre-emptee as petitioner filed the present revisional application and obtained Rule.

8. Mr Kazi Md Shafiqul Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioner in support of the Rule submits that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the case holding and as such the Courts below ought to have disallowed pre-emption. He further submits that none of the Courts below discussed evidence and as such the impugned judgments having been passed in a slip-shod manner are liable to be set aside. At the lag end of his submissions the learned Advocate for the petitioner came up with an alternative prayer to send back the case on remand to the trial Court for fresh trial on the ground that his client could not put up his defence case by examining OPWs and adducing documentary evidence because of illness on the dates fixed for hearing of the case. In this connection he further submits that on 30-10-2007 his client filed an application before the trial Court for adjournment of the hearing of the case on the ground of illness and a medical certificate was submitted in support of that application for adjournment, and the trial Court committed a serious illegality in rejecting the said application for adjournment since the same was supported by a medical certificate issued by a qualified physician.

9. On the other hand, Mr Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1 submits that the pre-emptee accepted the trial Court's order rejecting his application for adjournment since he did not invoke the jurisdiction of the higher Court against the said rejection order. He further submits that the pre-emptee-petitioner also did not take any step before the lower appellate Court to put up his defence case although he had ample opportunity to adduce addition evidence before the said court in support of his case and that having not been done before the Courts below, the pre-emptee-petitioner has waived his right to establish his defence. On this point Mr Bhuiyan next submits that the trial Court's order rejecting the pre-emptee's application for adjournment is not an issue before this Court and the same is beyond the terms of the present Rule and this Court in exercise of it supervisory jurisdiction cannot super-impose itself to ascertain the trial Court's order rejecting application for adjournment since the pre-emptee has accepted the said order long ago.

10. I have carefully examined the revisional application, the papers and documents annexed thereto, heard the learned Advocates for both the sides at length and perused the decisions and the relevant provisions of law.

11. It appears from the record that on 7-10-2007 the pre-emptee-petitioner was examined-in-chief in part and on the subsequent dates he did not make himself available before the trial Court for completion of his remaining examination-in-chief and cross-examination and he also refrained from adducing any documentary evidence in support of his defence case and therefore, he miserably failed to establish his defence plea to withstand pre-emption. In this regard Mr Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan submits that there exists a large number of case law which suggests that mere pleadings are no evidence unless the contents thereof are proved by examining witnesses on oath. In support of this submission Mr Bhuiyan has referred to a good number of decisions as reported in 16 BLD 519, 21 BLT (AD) 411, 34 BLD 55 and 4 X-File-1. It seems to be profitable to quote the ratio of the case of Md Serajul Islam vs Hosneara Begum reported in 34 BLD 55, which runs as follows:

"The filing of the written-statement without giving any oral testimony in support of the same before of the Court below and without facing cross-examination the same will not be considered ipso facto as evidence, rather, either of the pleadings must be proved by giving oral evidence."

<u>12. Thus, it manifestly appears that pre-emptee was altogether negligent and lethargic to pursue his defence case before the Courts below, which went on to dispose of the case on the basis of the pleadings of the respective parties, evidence adduced by the plaintiff and other materials on record in appreciation whereof they concurrently held that as a co-sharer by inheritance and by purchase the pre-emptor is entitled to pre-empt the case land and as a stranger the pre-emptee has got no locus standi to oppose the pre-emptor's statutory right of pre-emption and as such there is no scope to send back the case on remand to the trial court for fresh trial in the wake of the concurrent findings of the Courts below.</u>

13. On perusal of the record and evidence, I am of the considered view that the concurrent judgments and order of the courts below are very much sound, proper and in accordance with law and they do not suffer from any misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration or misconstruction of any document affecting the merit of the case and as such the same are binding upon me and hence, I find no minimum reason to interfere with the impugned judgments and order.

14. In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

15. The impugned judgment and order dated 15-3-2009 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Jessore in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 81 of 2007 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 8-11-2007 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Bagharpara, Jessore in Miscellaneous Case No. 23 of 2005 is hereby affirmed.

The stay granted earlier at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Send down the lower Court record, at once.

End.
